                        PROJECT NO. 58000
 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE          §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL      §                        OF TEXAS
 TRANSMISSION COST             §
 RECOVERY                      §
 IN THE ERCOT REGION

                  COMMENTS OF MODERN TEX CONSULTING LLC

ON THE JURISDICTIONAL SCOPE AND STATUTORY PRECISION OF PROPOSED

                  16 TAC §25.192 AS APPLIED TO NON-IOU UTILITIES


TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

   Modern Tex Consulting LLC submits these comments on the July 9, 2026 proposal for

publication of amendments to 16 Texas Administrative Code §§25.192 and 25.193 and proposed

new §25.252 (the PFP).

   The record presents difficult policy choices. Commenters disagree about whether twelve

coincident peaks are too many, whether a minimum billing demand should be 100% or 75%,

whether it should last twenty years or ten, and whether batch-study costs belong with an

individual customer or the broader transmission system. Modern Tex takes no position on any of

those disputes.

   Its concern is more basic: whatever policy the Commission selects must be expressed in a

rule that applies coherently to every covered entity and remains within the authority the

Legislature granted. That concern is not Modern Tex’s alone. On the four points below,

Modern Tex’s position is shared by the very Non-IOU utilities the rule would govern—the

Public Power Utilities (Item 17), CPS Energy (Item 21), Guadalupe Valley Electric Cooperative

(Item 19), and the statewide association Texas Electric Cooperatives (Item 30)—and, on the
 most important jurisdictional point, by a consumer and environmental commenter with no utility

stake at all (Sierra Club, Item 18).

   Modern Tex respectfully proposes four narrow refinements:

   1. Strike proposed §25.192(c)(2) and the related §25.192(b)(15)–(16) definitions as

       applied to Non-IOU TSPs, or expressly exempt them, because the wholesale-

       transmission-service-at-distribution-voltage (WTS-DV) tariff requirement reaches

       distribution service and pricing that PURA reserves to the governing bodies of

       municipally owned utilities and electric cooperatives;

   2. Correct §25.192(f)(1)(B) so that the large-load minimum billing demand is defined and

       administrable for Non-IOU DSPs whose service is not governed by §25.193;

   3. Confirm that §25.192(f)(1)(A) is limited to meter data reasonably necessary for

       ERCOT’s 12CP calculation and associated administration, and does not expand

       Commission jurisdiction over Non-IOU retail rate design; and

   4. Clarify the rule’s application to river authorities by identifying, requirement by

       requirement, the statutory basis for the Commission’s authority and explaining whether

       any proposed requirement directly or indirectly regulates matters protected by PURA

       §32.051.

   These refinements do not alter 12CP, the minimum billing demand, or any other policy

choice at the center of Senate Bill 6. They simply make the rule say clearly who must do what,

under which statute, and within what jurisdictional boundary. This is a request to tighten the

bolts, not to redesign the engine.

I. INTEREST OF THE COMMENTER
    Modern Tex is a newly formed policy advisory and consulting firm concerned with the

lawful, administrable, and transparent implementation of Texas energy policy in the ERCOT
 region. Modern Tex submits these comments on its own behalf. These comments were not

commissioned or funded by any client, and Modern Tex neither represents a party in this

proceeding nor offers coincident-peak curtailment or transmission-cost-avoidance services.

   That position allows Modern Tex to occupy a useful role in this record. Modern Tex does not

benefit from selecting one minimum-billing percentage, one coincident-peak configuration, or

one cost-allocation outcome over another. Its interest is ensuring that the Commission’s chosen

policy rests on identified statutory authority, works for every entity to which it applies, and can

be administered without future proceedings to resolve today’s avoidable ambiguities.

   Modern Tex commends the Commission and Staff for the care reflected in this proposal.

Implementing Senate Bill 6 is demanding work. The Commission must accommodate

extraordinary load growth, protect existing customers from cost shifts, preserve ERCOT

reliability, and maintain a workable investment environment. Modern Tex offers these comments

in that same constructive spirit—as a partner in helping a consequential rule land on the firmest

possible legal ground.

II. THE RECORD REVEALS BROAD AGREEMENT THAT SEVERAL PROVISIONS
REQUIRE CLARIFICATION BEFORE ADOPTION
    The comments filed in this project disagree sharply on policy. On the large-load minimum

billing demand, GVEC (Item 19), CPS Energy (Item 21), the City of Houston (Item 24), Texas

Electric Cooperatives (Item 30), and the Environmental Defense Fund (Item 28) support a strong

floor keyed to contracted peak demand. The ERCOT Steel Mills (Item 27), TAEBA (Item 25),

Conservative Texans for Energy Innovation (Item 26), Voltus (Item 16), the individual

commenters in Items 13 and 22, and the Sierra Club (Item 18) urge a lower percentage, a shorter

term, or a phased reduction. The Texas Energy Buyers Alliance study by J. Pollock (Item 12)

identifies roughly 75% to 80% of contracted demand as the rate-neutral range, while H-E-B and
 STEC (Item 31) would abandon coincident peaks altogether in favor of a non-coincident-peak

metric. Item 20 collects roughly 350 individual consumer letters. Modern Tex takes no position

within that debate.

   But beneath that disagreement runs a striking area of consensus: commenters across every

camp report that specific provisions must be clarified before adoption.

   •   Hunt Energy Network (Item 29) explains that the unqualified phrase “interconnection

       agreements” in §25.192(e)(6) could unintentionally reach generation-interconnection

       agreements governed by a separate framework, and proposes a narrow edit tying the

       provision to large-load agreements under §25.194.

   •   EDF (Item 28) identifies two facially plausible readings of §25.193(d)(3)—one tying

       billing to service actually made available, the other requiring billing on full contracted

       load before service is available.

   •   CTEI (Item 26) and the ERCOT Steel Mills (Item 27) identify uncertainty created by

       cross-references to §§25.194 and 25.252, some not yet finally adopted, governing

       capacity reservation and reallocation.

   •   American Bitcoin (Item 14), Hut 8 (Item 15), and CPS Energy (Item 21) each warn

       that §25.192(k) may permit the same interconnection costs to be recovered twice—once

       under §25.194 and again through rates—and ask for an express credit.

   •   Texas Electric Cooperatives (Item 30) documents pervasive inconsistency in the PFP’s

       use of “IOU,” “non-IOU,” “TSP,” and “DSP,” warning that the drafting creates “a risk

       that an electric cooperative or municipally owned utility is pulled into an investor-owned-

       utility-specific obligation by imprecise drafting rather than by design—and that risk is

       highest in precisely the provisions where the Commission drew jurisdictional lines.”
    Modern Tex’s concerns belong to that same family, but carry an added consequence. An

ambiguous term may produce administrative confusion. A cross-reference to a rule that does not

govern the covered entity may leave a required calculation undefined. And language that

assumes identical authority over legally distinct entities may cause the rule to exceed the

jurisdiction the Legislature provided. The remedy in every case is the same: complete the

connective work—define the operative terms, align the cross-references, identify the authority

applicable to each entity, and state the boundaries the proposal now leaves to inference.

III. A DISTRIBUTION REQUIREMENT CANNOT ACQUIRE TRANSMISSION
AUTHORITY MERELY BY BEING PLACED IN §25.192
    Modern Tex joins the Public Power Utilities (Item 17), CPS Energy (Item 21), and Texas

Electric Cooperatives (Item 30) in asking the Commission to strike proposed §25.192(c)(2)—and

the related WTS-DV definitions in §25.192(b)(15)–(16)—as applied to Non-IOU TSPs, or

expressly exempt them. This is not a solitary concern. The Public Power Utilities devote their

entire filing to it. CPS Energy files separately to the same effect, objecting to the “implied

expansion of Commission jurisdiction… into MOU distribution ratemaking.” TEC, the statewide

cooperative association, devotes a full section to it and proposes conforming rule text. And the

Sierra Club, a consumer and environmental commenter with no ratemaking stake, independently

volunteers that the provision “might exceed PUCT authority” and suggests the Commission

confirm its statutory footing. When the regulated utilities, their statewide association, and a

consumer advocate independently reach the same jurisdictional conclusion, the Commission

should take the signal seriously.

   The issue is not whether a WTS-DV tariff might be administratively useful. CTEI (Item 26)

supports requiring a timely WTS-DV tariff and even suggests a uniform interconnection

agreement. A uniform tariff may indeed be convenient. But administrative usefulness does not
 supply statutory authority, and uniformity cannot erase the jurisdictional lines the Legislature

drew.

    Proposed §25.192 is the Commission’s transmission-service rule. Section 25.192(c)(2),

however, would require a tariff addressing wholesale transmission service delivered at

distribution voltage, including the cost of distribution-level facilities and service. For

municipally owned utilities and electric cooperatives, PURA assigns jurisdiction over those

distribution terms and rates to their governing bodies. PURA §40.055(a)(1) grants a municipal

governing body “exclusive jurisdiction” over the utility’s rates and services, and PURA

§41.055(1) gives a cooperative’s board the same “exclusive jurisdiction.” The operative word is

exclusive. A general transmission provision cannot annex authority the Legislature expressly

assigned elsewhere.

    The Texas Supreme Court has drawn this boundary twice. In Public Utility Commission of

Texas v. City Public Service Board of San Antonio, the Court held that Commission jurisdiction

over municipally owned utilities “is restricted” and that such utilities “retain the ability to set

their own rates without the Commission’s approval.” 53 S.W.3d 310, 318 (Tex. 2001). In Texas

Municipal Power Agency v. Public Utility Commission of Texas, the Court held that “[n]owhere

does PURA chapter 35 give the Commission general rate oversight capacity” over such a utility,

describing the agency’s role as “largely an oversight role.” 253 S.W.3d 184, 194 (Tex. 2007). As

both the Public Power Utilities and TEC observe, the Commission’s authority over these entities

under PURA §35.004(a) is confined to ensuring open, comparable wholesale transmission

access—not conducting distribution cost-of-service ratemaking.

    Nor is this only a problem of abstract jurisdiction. As the Public Power Utilities and TEC

both document, the Commission has for more than two decades kept TCOS proceedings under
 §25.192 separate from WTS-DV tariff proceedings under §25.191, and the two rules recover

different costs recorded in different FERC accounts. The Commission itself has recognized that

“a tariff for wholesale transmission service at distribution voltage under §25.191 differs from a

tariff for transmission service under §25.192.” Medina Elec. Coop., Docket No. 51606,

Preliminary Order at 2 (June 14, 2021). The proposal would depart from that settled practice

without identifying a statute, policy need, or changed circumstance requiring the change.

   If the Commission believes a uniform WTS-DV framework is necessary, that subject

deserves a dedicated proceeding in which the Commission can identify the relevant statutory

authority, distinguish IOUs from Non-IOUs, and provide focused notice to the entities whose

distribution authority is implicated. The cleaner course in this proceeding is to strike

§25.192(c)(2) and its associated definitions as applied to Non-IOU TSPs, or expressly exempt

them—precisely the relief the affected utilities request.

IV. SECTION 25.192(f)(1)(B) POINTS NON-IOUs TO A RULE THAT DOES NOT
GOVERN THEM
   The problem with §25.192(f)(1)(B) is simpler, and it is not Modern Tex’s invention. Both

major Non-IOUs to address it—GVEC (Item 19) and CPS Energy (Item 21)—identify the same

defect and ask for the same fix.

   The provision directs ERCOT to adjust each DSP’s 12CP load by reference to each large-

load customer’s “large load minimum billing demand… as described in §25.193.” But §25.193

governs IOU DSP transmission-cost recovery. As GVEC explains, §25.193 “by its terms applies

only to investor-owned DSPs,” so “for a non-IOU DSP’s large load, no §25.193 value

necessarily exists, leaving the wholesale adjustment mechanism undefined for cooperatives.”

CPS Energy makes the identical point: “current language references §25.193, which is not
 applicable to Non-IOU DSPs,” and recommends “relocating large load minimum billing demand

provisions from §25.193(d)(2) to §25.192(f)(1)(B).”

   The reference works for an IOU DSP. It does not work for a municipally owned utility or

electric cooperative whose retail service §25.193 does not govern. And the gap is not cured by

assuming the IOU formula will simply be imported into the Non-IOU calculation. If that is the

Commission’s intent, the rule should say so and identify the authority under which the common

wholesale determinant is established. A required ERCOT calculation should not depend on

implication from a retail rule that does not apply to the entity supplying the data.

   Other commenters have flagged the same species of scope error. Hunt Energy Network’s

proposed correction to §25.192(e)(6) (Item 29) follows the right model: name the intended

category in the text and eliminate the unintended reading without changing the policy. The

Commission can correct §25.192(f)(1)(B) in either of two ways:

   1. Move the minimum-billing-demand provisions necessary for the wholesale adjustment

       into §25.192(f)(1)(B), where they will apply to all DSPs covered by the adjustment—the

       relocation CPS Energy recommends; or

   2. Add a separate definition for Non-IOU DSPs that identifies the applicable determinant—

       drawn, as GVEC suggests, from contracted peak demand or available service under

       §25.194 and the interconnection agreement required by §25.252—without making their

       retail service subject to §25.193.

   This is housekeeping, not policy. Commenters may continue to disagree about whether the

determinant should be 100%, 75%, phased, weighted, or ratcheted. Modern Tex takes no position

on that choice. Its point is only that once the Commission selects the number, §25.192 must

define that number for every DSP required to use it.
 V. THE METER-DATA REQUIREMENT SHOULD BE RETAINED AND BOUNDED
   Modern Tex does not ask the Commission to strike §25.192(f)(1)(A). Settlement-quality

meter data is necessary for ERCOT to perform the 12CP adjustment and to verify large-load

demand, and the record confirms its value. GVEC (Item 19) expressly “does not oppose” the

requirement; TEC (Item 30) states its members “do not object to sharing or providing access to

such data”; and TAEBA (Item 25) and the individual commenters in Items 13 and 22 emphasize

that interval data is foundational to both cost allocation and reliability-program measurement. No

affected utility has treated the data obligation itself as equivalent to Commission control over its

retail rates.

    What the affected utilities ask for is a boundary—and they ask for it in nearly the terms

Modern Tex proposes. GVEC requests that the Commission “confirm on the record that this data

obligation is limited to what is necessary to perform the 12CP adjustment and does not expand

the Commission’s jurisdiction over GVEC’s retail rate design or class structure.” CPS Energy

(Item 21) and TEC (Item 30) raise parallel concerns about timing, formats, cybersecurity,

confidentiality, undefined use of the word “timely,” and routing the data through the

cooperative’s TSP or transmission operator. Modern Tex asks the Commission to grant that

boundary.

    The obligation should reach the settlement-quality data reasonably necessary for ERCOT to

calculate and administer the 12CP adjustment and other expressly authorized wholesale

functions. It should not become an independent basis for Commission oversight of a Non-IOU’s

retail customer classifications, class-cost allocation, or rate design. The Commission can draw

that line in a single sentence in the adoption preamble:
           Nothing in §25.192(f)(1)(A) expands the Commission’s jurisdiction over the retail rates,

          rate design, customer classifications, or class-cost allocation of a municipally owned

          utility, electric cooperative, or river authority.

   The Commission should also define “timely” and “settlement-quality,” rely on ERCOT’s

existing registration and metering processes where practicable, and preserve the confidentiality

of competitively sensitive large-load and member information—each a guardrail the affected

utilities themselves requested.

VI. RIVER AUTHORITIES REQUIRE AN ENTITY-SPECIFIC STATUTORY
ANALYSIS
   On the first three points, Modern Tex reinforces concerns the affected utilities have already

raised. This fourth point stands apart: of the nineteen substantive filings in this record, only one

even notices the issue, and none completes the analysis.

   The proposed rule’s “Non-IOU” label groups river authorities with municipally owned

utilities and electric cooperatives. Proposed §25.192(b)(10)–(11) define both “non-IOU DSP”

and “non-IOU TSP” to include a “municipally owned utility, river authority, or electric

cooperative,” and every operative requirement then applies to the combined class without

distinction. Texas Electric Cooperatives observed the resulting tension—noting that PURA’s

defined term “electric utility” excludes “municipally owned utilities, electric cooperatives, and

river authorities,” and warning that imprecise entity terminology risks pulling a Non-IOU into an

IOU-specific obligation. Item 30, at 9. But TEC did not identify the statutory authority the

Commission relies on for river authorities, and no commenter—including TEC—has addressed

whether PURA §32.051 limits any proposed requirement. That analysis remains undone on this

record.
     A regulatory label is not a grant of statutory authority. An agency possesses only the powers

conferred by the Legislature, together with implied powers reasonably necessary to carry out its

express responsibilities. Texas Municipal Power Agency, 253 S.W.3d at 192–94. And even

within a transmission rulemaking, the Commission’s authority over a Non-IOU entity must be

traced to the statutes governing that entity. City Public Service Board, 53 S.W.3d at 315–19.

River authorities occupy a distinct legal position: they are constitutionally created conservation

and reclamation districts governed in part by entity-specific enabling legislation, not merely

another form of municipal or cooperative utility. Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authority, No.

24-9101, slip op. at 2–6 (Tex. June 27, 2025) (per curiam).

    That distinct status matters because PURA §32.051 expressly limits Commission authority

over a defined category of river authorities and activities. Section 32.051 does not exempt every

river authority from every Commission rule. It applies to a river authority that operated a steam-

generating plant on or before January 1, 1999, and protects specified matters related to the

generation and sale of electricity at wholesale. But within that sphere, the Legislature used

unusually comprehensive language: notwithstanding any other provision of PURA, the

Commission may not directly or indirectly regulate the covered revenue requirements, rates,

fuel costs, fuel charges, or fuel acquisitions.

    Staff’s own Statutory Authority statement sharpens the problem. It invokes PURA §32.001’s

“exclusive original jurisdiction” over an electric utility, but it neither identifies any authority

specific to river authorities nor addresses §32.051. A river authority may fall within the “electric

utility” definition in some respects while §32.051 simultaneously withdraws the Commission’s

authority to regulate—directly or indirectly—its protected wholesale-generation matters. The

general grant does not answer the specific question.
    Modern Tex recognizes that the Commission has express authority over wholesale

transmission service in ERCOT and implied powers reasonably necessary to carry out that

responsibility. Modern Tex does not contend that §32.051 converts a defined generation-related

limitation into general immunity from transmission regulation. But broad transmission authority

does not eliminate a specific statutory restriction, and the question cannot be resolved merely by

labeling the proposal a transmission rule. Because §32.051 reaches indirect as well as direct

regulation, the Commission should consider each requirement’s operation and effect, and should

identify:

   1. the statutory authority supporting each proposed requirement as applied to river

       authorities;

   2. whether the requirement applies to a river authority qualifying under §32.051; and

   3. whether the requirement directly or indirectly affects the protected revenue requirements,

       rates, fuel costs, fuel charges, or fuel acquisitions associated with that river authority’s

       wholesale-generation activities.

   If §32.051 has no effect on a particular requirement, the Commission can explain why. If the

statute limits only a particular application, the final rule can draw that boundary expressly.

Modern Tex does not request a categorical exemption; a reasoned explanation in the adoption

preamble would suffice. But the common “Non-IOU” label cannot substitute for the analysis.

VII. THE UNIFYING PRINCIPLE: USEFULNESS IS NOT AUTHORITY, AND A
CROSS-REFERENCE IS NOT A DEFINITION
   One principle connects these comments. A policy may be useful without being authorized as

applied to every entity. A term may be understandable in an IOU rule without being defined for a

Non-IOU. A data requirement may be lawful for administering a wholesale calculation without
 opening the door to retail-rate regulation. And a transmission label does not, by itself, resolve

whether a requirement indirectly reaches a statutorily protected generation matter.

   The broader record confirms that careful final drafting is not a cosmetic concern. Across

filings that otherwise disagree on nearly everything, commenters have identified terms that could

reach the wrong agreements (Item 29), provisions that admit conflicting readings (Item 28),

obligations whose meaning depends on unfinished or entity-specific cross-references (Items 14,

15, 21, 26, 27), pervasive inconsistency in the very IOU/Non-IOU terminology that marks the

Commission’s jurisdictional lines (Item 30), and—most directly relevant here—Non-IOU

provisions that the affected utilities and a consumer advocate believe may exceed the

Commission’s authority (Items 17, 18, 21, and 30). Modern Tex asks the Commission to apply

the same disciplined solution to the Non-IOU provisions:

   1. Strike or exempt Non-IOU TSPs from §25.192(c)(2) and its associated definitions;

   2. Define the §25.192(f)(1)(B) billing determinant for every covered DSP;

   3. Bound §25.192(f)(1)(A) to its authorized wholesale purpose; and

   4. Identify the authority applicable to river authorities and explain the operation of §32.051.

   None of these refinements requires the Commission to choose between GVEC and the Steel

Mills, between Houston and TAEBA, or between a 100% floor and a 75% floor. They hold true

under any policy outcome the Commission adopts.

VIII. CONCLUSION
   This record gives the Commission no shortage of policy advice—competing percentages,

alternative coincident-peak structures, proposed cost-allocation tests, empirical studies, detailed

redlines, and roughly 350 individual consumer letters. Modern Tex offers something different:

four legal and drafting refinements that remain necessary regardless of which policy choices the
 Commission ultimately makes, and that reinforce concerns the affected Non-IOU utilities have

themselves placed in the record.

   The Commission should not require a Non-IOU to file a distribution tariff through a

transmission proceeding without identifying authority over the distribution rates involved. It

should not direct ERCOT to calculate a Non-IOU adjustment through a rule that does not govern

the entity. It should not leave the jurisdictional boundary of a mandatory data obligation to

implication. And it should not treat river authorities as interchangeable with cities and

cooperatives without addressing the statutes applicable to that distinct class.

   Modern Tex therefore respectfully requests that the Commission:

   1. strike proposed §25.192(c)(2) and its associated definitions as applied to Non-IOU TSPs

       or expressly exempt them;

   2. correct §25.192(f)(1)(B) so the minimum billing demand is defined for Non-IOU DSPs;

   3. confirm that §25.192(f)(1)(A) does not expand Commission jurisdiction over Non-IOU

       retail rate design; and

   4. identify, requirement by requirement, the statutory authority applicable to river

       authorities and explain whether any requirement directly or indirectly regulates matters

       protected by PURA §32.051.

   These changes would not weaken Senate Bill 6 or delay its implementation. They would give

the Commission a rule that is clearer to regulated entities, easier for ERCOT to administer, and

more durable on judicial review. Modern Tex supports the Commission’s work and respectfully

asks only that a strong policy finish with equally strong statutory drafting.

Dated: August 11, 2026

Respectfully submitted,
 Raven S. Kyles

Modern Tex Consulting LLC

        use of"IOU,   '5"
                            non-IOU,   '5"
                                             TSP," and "DSP," warning that the drafting creates "a risk

        that an electric cooperative or municipally owned utility is pulled into an investor-owned-

        utility-specific obligation by imprecise drafting rather than by design-and that risk is

        highest in precisely the provisions where the Commission drew jurisdictional lines."
    Modern Tex' s concerns belong to that same family, but carry an added consequence. An

ambiguous term may produce administrative confusion. A cross-reference to a rule that does not

govern the covered entity may leave a required calculation undefined. And language that

assumes identical authority over legally distinct entities may cause the rule to exceed the

jurisdiction the Legislature provided. The remedy in every case is the same: complete the

connective work-define the operative terms, align the cross-references, identify the authority

applicable to each entity, and state the boundaries the proposal now leaves to inference.

III. A DISTRIBUTION REQUIREMENT CANNOT ACQUIRE TRANSMISSION
AUTHORITY MERELY BY BEING PLACED IN §25.192
    Modern Tex joins the Public Power Utilities (Item 17), CPS Energy (Item 21), and Texas

Electric Cooperatives (Item 30) in asking the Commission to strike proposed §25.192(c)(2)-and

the related WTS-DV definitions in §25.192(b)(15)-(16)-as applied to Non-IOU TSPs, or

expressly exempt them. This is not a solitary concern. The Public Power Utilities devote their

entire filing to it. CPS Energy files separately to the same effect, objecting to the "implied

expansion of Commission jurisdiction... into MOU distribution ratemaking." TEC, the statewide

cooperative association, devotes a full section to it and proposes conforming rule text. And the

Sierra Club, a consumer and environmental commenter with no ratemaking stake, independently

volunteers that the provision "might exceed PUCT authority" and suggests the Commission

confirm its statutory footing. When the regulated utilities, their statewide association, and a

consumer advocate independently reach the same jurisdictional conclusion, the Commission

should take the signal seriously.

    The issue is not whether a WTS-DV tariff might be administratively useful. CTEI (Item 26)

supports requiring a timely WTS-DV tariff and even suggests a uniform interconnection

agreement. A uniform tariff may indeed be convenient. But administrative usefulness does not
 supply statutory authority, and uniformity cannot erase the jurisdictional lines the Legislature

drew.

   Proposed §25.192 is the Commission's transmission-service rule. Section 25.192(c)(2),

however, would require a tariff addressing wholesale transmission service delivered at

distribution voltage, including the cost of distribution-level facilities and service. For

municipally owned utilities and electric cooperatives, PURA assigns jurisdiction over those

distribution terms and rates to their governing bodies. PURA §40.055(a)(1) grants a municipal

governing body "exclusive jurisdiction" over the utility' s rates and services, and PURA

§41.055(1) gives a cooperative's board the same "exclusive jurisdiction." The operative word is

exclusive. A general transmission provision cannot annex authority the Legislature expressly

assigned elsewhere.

    The Texas Supreme Court has drawn this boundary twice . In Public Utility Commission of

Texas v. City Public Service Board of San Antonio, the Court held that Commission jurisdiction

over municipally owned utilities "is restricted" and that such utilities "retain the ability to set

their own rates without the Commission's approval." 53 S.W.3d 310, 318 (Tex. 2001). In Texas

Municipal Power Agency v. Public Utility Commission of Texas, the Courtheld that"Inlowhere

does PURA chapter 35 give the Commission general rate oversight capacity" over such a utility,

describing the agency's role as "largely an oversight role." 253 S.W.3d 184, 194 (Tex. 2007). As

both the Public Power Utilities and TEC observe, the Commission' s authority over these entities

under PURA §35.004(a) is confined to ensuring open, comparable wholesale transmission

access-not conducting distribution cost-of-service ratemaking.

   Nor is this only a problem of abstract jurisdiction. As the Public Power Utilities and TEC

both document, the Commission has for more than two decades kept TCOS proceedings under
 §25.192 separate from WTS-DV tariff proceedings under §25.191, and the two rules recover

different costs recorded in different FERC accounts. The Commission itself has recognized that

"a tariff for wholesale transmission service at distribution voltage under §25.191 differs from a

tariff for transmission service under § 25 . 192 ." Medina Elec. Coop., Docket No . 51606 ,

Preliminary Order at 2 (June 14,2021). The proposal would depart from that settled practice

without identifying a statute, policy need, or changed circumstance requiring the change.

   If the Commission believes a uniform WTS-DV framework is necessary, that subject

deserves a dedicated proceeding in which the Commission can identify the relevant statutory

authority, distinguish IOUs from Non-IOUs, and provide focused notice to the entities whose

distribution authority is implicated. The cleaner course in this proceeding is to strike

§25.192(c)(2) and its associated definitions as applied to Non-IOU TSPs, or expressly exempt

them-precisely the relief the affected utilities request.

IV. SECTION 25.192(f)(1)(B) POINTS NON-IOUs TO A RULE THAT DOES NOT
GOVERN THEM
   The problem with §25.192(f)(1)(B) is simpler, and it is not Modern Tex' s invention. Both

major Non-IOUs to address it-GVEC (Item 19) and CPS Energy (Item 21)-identify the same

defect and ask for the same fix.

    The provision directs ERCOT to adjust each DSP' s 12CP load by reference to each large-

load customer's "large load minimum billing demand... as described in §25.193." But §25.193

governs IOU DSP transmission-cost recovery. As GVEC explains, §25.193 "by its terms applies

only to investor-owned DSPs," so "for a non-IOU DSP's large load, no §25.193 value

necessarily exists, leaving the wholesale adjustment mechanism undefined for cooperatives."

CPS Energy makes the identical point: "current language references §25.193, which is not
 applicable to Non-IOU DSPs," and recommends "relocating large load minimum billing demand

provisions from §25.193(d)(2) to §25.192(f)(1)(B)."

   The reference works for an IOU DSP. It does not work for a municipally owned utility or

electric cooperative whose retail service §25.193 does not govern. And the gap is not cured by

assuming the IOU formula will simply be imported into the Non-IOU calculation. If that is the

Commission' s intent, the rule should say so and identify the authority under which the common

wholesale determinant is established. A required ERCOT calculation should not depend on

implication from a retail rule that does not apply to the entity supplying the data.

   Other commenters have flagged the same species of scope error. Hunt Energy Network' s

proposed correction to §25.192(e)(6) (Item 29) follows the right model: name the intended

category in the text and eliminate the unintended reading without changing the policy. The

Commission can correct §25.192(f)(1)(B) in either of two ways:

    1. Move the minimum-billing-demand provisions necessary for the wholesale adjustment

       into §25.192(f)(1)(B), where they will apply to all DSPs covered by the adjustment-the

       relocation CPS Energy recommends; or

   2. Add a separate definition for Non-IOU DSPs that identifies the applicable determinant-

       drawn, as GVEC suggests, from contracted peak demand or available service under

        §25.194 and the interconnection agreement required by §25.252-without making their

       retail service subject to §25.193.

   This is housekeeping, not policy. Commenters may continue to disagree about whether the

determinant should be 100%, 75%, phased, weighted, or ratcheted. Modern Tex takes no position

on that choice. Its point is only that once the Commission selects the number, §25.192 must

define that number for every DSP required to use it.
 V. THE METER-DATA REQUIREMENT SHOULD BE RETAINED AND BOUNDED
   Modern Tex does not ask the Commission to strike §25.192(f)(1)(A). Settlement-quality

meter data is necessary for ERCOT to perform the 12CP adjustment and to verify large-load

demand, and the record confirms its value. GVEC (Item 19) expressly "does not oppose" the

requirement; TEC (Item 30) states its members "do not object to sharing or providing access to

such data" ; and TAEBA (Item 25) and the individual commenters in Items 13 and 22 emphasize

that interval data is foundational to both cost allocation and reliability-program measurement. No

affected utility has treated the data obligation itself as equivalent to Commission control over its

retail rates.

    What the affected utilities ask for is a boundary-and they ask for it in nearly the terms

Modern Tex proposes. GVEC requests that the Commission "confirm on the record that this data

obligation is limited to what is necessary to perform the 12CP adjustment and does not expand

the Commission's jurisdiction over GVEC's retail rate design or class structure." CPS Energy

(Item 21) and TEC (Item 30) raise parallel concerns about timing, formats, cybersecurity,

confidentiality, undefined use of the word "timely," and routing the data through the

cooperative' s TSP or transmission operator. Modern Tex asks the Commission to grant that

boundary.

    The obligation should reach the settlement-quality data reasonably necessary for ERCOT to

calculate and administer the 12CP adjustment and other expressly authorized wholesale

functions. It should not become an independent basis for Commission oversight of a Non-IOU' s

retail customer classifications, class-cost allocation, or rate design. The Commission can draw

that line in a single sentence in the adoption preamble:
           Nothing in §25.192*(1)(A) expands the Commission'sjurisdiction over the retail rates,

          rate design, customer classifications, or class-cost allocation ofa municipally owned

          utility, electric cooperative, or river authority.

    The Commission should also define "timely" and "settlement-quality," rely on ERCOT' s

existing registration and metering processes where practicable, and preserve the confidentiality

of competitively sensitive large-load and member information-each a guardrail the affected

utilities themselves requested.

VI. RIVER AUTHORITIES REQUIRE AN ENTITY-SPECIFIC STATUTORY
ANALYSIS
   On the first three points, Modern Tex reinforces concerns the affected utilities have already

raised. This fourth point stands apart: of the nineteen substantive filings in this record, only one

even notices the issue, and none completes the analysis.

    The proposed rule's "Non-IOU" label groups river authorities with municipally owned

utilities and electric cooperatives. Proposed §25.192(b)(10)-(11) define both "non-IOU DSP"

and "non-IOU TSP" to include a "municipally owned utility, river authority, or electric

cooperative," and every operative requirement then applies to the combined class without

distinction. Texas Electric Cooperatives observed the resulting tension-noting that PURA' s

defined term "electric utility" excludes "municipally owned utilities, electric cooperatives, and

river authorities," and warning that imprecise entity terminology risks pulling a Non-IOU into an

IOU-specific obligation. Item 30, at 9. But TEC did not identify the statutory authority the

Commission relies on for river authorities, and no commenter-including TEC-has addressed

whether PURA §32.051 limits any proposed requirement. That analysis remains undone on this

record.
     A regulatory label is not a grant of statutory authority. An agency possesses only the powers

conferred by the Legislature, together with implied powers reasonably necessary to carry out its

express responsibilities. TexasMunicipal Power Agency, 253 S.W.3d at 192-94. And even

within a transmission rulemaking, the Commission' s authority over a Non-IOU entity must be

traced to the statutes governing that entity. Cio, Public Service Board, 53 S.W.3d at 315-19.

River authorities occupy a distinct legal position: they are constitutionally created conservation

and reclamation districts governed in part by entity-specific enabling legislation, not merely

another form of municipal or cooperative utility. Baumgardner v. Brazos River Authorio/, No.

24-9101, slip op. at 2-6 (Tex. June 27, 2025) (per curiam).

    That distinct status matters because PURA §32.051 expressly limits Commission authority

over a defined category of river authorities and activities. Section 32.051 does not exempt every

river authority from every Commission rule. It applies to a river authority that operated a steam-

generating plant on or before January 1, 1999, and protects specified matters related to the

generation and sale of electricity at wholesale. But within that sphere, the Legislature used

unusually comprehensive language: notwithstanding any other provision of PURA, the

Commission may not directly or indirectly regulate the covered revenue requirements, rates,

fuel costs, fuel charges, or fuel acquisitions.

    Staff' s own Statutory Authority statement sharpens the problem. It invokes PURA §32.001' s

"exclusive original jurisdiction" over an electric utility, but it neither identifies any authority

specific to river authorities nor addresses §32.051. A river authority may fall within the "electric

utility" definition in some respects while §32.051 simultaneously withdraws the Commission's

authority to regulate-directly or indirectly-its protected wholesale-generation matters. The

general grant does not answer the specific question.
     Modern Tex recognizes that the Commission has express authority over wholesale

transmission service in ERCOT and implied powers reasonably necessary to carry out that

responsibility. Modern Tex does not contend that §32.051 converts a defined generation-related

limitation into general immunity from transmission regulation. But broad transmission authority

does not eliminate a specific statutory restriction, and the question cannot be resolved merely by

labeling the proposal a transmission rule. Because §32.051 reaches indirect as well as direct

regulation, the Commission should consider each requirement' s operation and effect, and should

identify:

    1. the statutory authority supporting each proposed requirement as applied to river

        authorities;

    2. whether the requirement applies to a river authority qualifying under §32.051; and

    3. whether the requirement directly or indirectly affects the protected revenue requirements,

        rates, fuel costs, fuel charges, or fuel acquisitions associated with that river authority' s

        wholesale-generation activities.

    If §32.051 has no effect on a particular requirement, the Commission can explain why. If the

statute limits only a particular application, the final rule can draw that boundary expressly.

Modern Tex does not request a categorical exemption; a reasoned explanation in the adoption

preamble would suffice. But the common "Non-IOU" label cannot substitute for the analysis.

VII. THE UNIFYING PRINCIPLE: USEFULNESS IS NOT AUTHORITY, AND A
CROSS-REFERENCE IS NOT A DEFINITION
   One principle connects these comments. A policy may be useful without being authorized as

applied to every entity. A term may be understandable in an IOU rule without being defined for a

Non-IOU. A data requirement may be lawful for administering a wholesale calculation without
 opening the door to retail-rate regulation. And a transmission label does not, by itself, resolve

whether a requirement indirectly reaches a statutorily protected generation matter.

   The broader record confirms that careful final drafting is not a cosmetic concern. Across

filings that otherwise disagree on nearly everything, commenters have identified terms that could

reach the wrong agreements (Item 29), provisions that admit conflicting readings (Item 28),

obligations whose meaning depends on unfinished or entity-specific cross-references (Items 14,

15, 21, 26, 27), pervasive inconsistency in the very IOU/Non-IOU terminology that marks the

Commission' s jurisdictional lines (Item 30), and-most directly relevant here-Non-IOU

provisions that the affected utilities and a consumer advocate believe may exceed the

Commission' s authority (Items 17, 18,21, and 30). Modern Tex asks the Commission to apply

the same disciplined solution to the Non-IOU provisions:

    1. Strike or exempt Non-IOU TSPs from §25.192(c)(2) and its associated definitions;

   2. Define the §25.192(f)(1)(B) billing determinant for every covered DSP;

   3. Bound §25.192(f)(1)(A) to its authorized wholesale purpose; and

   4. Identify the authority applicable to river authorities and explain the operation of §32.051.

   None of these refinements requires the Commission to choose between GVEC and the Steel

Mills, between Houston and TAEBA, or between a 100% floor and a 75% floor. They hold true

under any policy outcome the Commission adopts.

VIII. CONCLUSION
   This record gives the Commission no shortage of policy advice--competing percentages,

alternative coincident-peak structures, proposed cost-allocation tests, empirical studies, detailed

redlines, and roughly 350 individual consumer letters. Modern Tex offers something different:

four legal and drafting refinements that remain necessary regardless of which policy choices the
 Commission ultimately makes, and that reinforce concerns the affected Non-IOU utilities have

themselves placed in the record.

   The Commission should not require a Non-IOU to file a distribution tariff through a

transmission proceeding without identifying authority over the distribution rates involved. It

should not direct ERCOT to calculate a Non-IOU adjustment through a rule that does not govern

the entity. It should not leave the jurisdictional boundary of a mandatory data obligation to

implication. And it should not treat river authorities as interchangeable with cities and

cooperatives without addressing the statutes applicable to that distinct class.

   Modern Tex therefore respectfully requests that the Commission:

    1. strike proposed §25.192(c)(2) and its associated definitions as applied to Non-IOU TSPs

       or expressly exempt them;

   2. correct §25.192(f)(1)(B) so the minimum billing demand is defined for Non-IOU DSPs;

   3. confirm that §25.192(f)(1)(A) does not expand Commission jurisdiction over Non-IOU

       retail rate design; and

   4. identify, requirement by requirement, the statutory authority applicable to river

       authorities and explain whether any requirement directly or indirectly regulates matters

       protected by PURA §32.051.

   These changes would not weaken Senate Bill 6 or delay its implementation. They would give

the Commission a rule that is clearer to regulated entities, easier for ERCOT to administer, and

more durable on judicial review. Modern Tex supports the Commission's work and respectfully

asks only that a strong policy finish with equally strong statutory drafting.
